text: Theodore Eliopoulos’s paper "Some observations on the iconography of the ‘Ring of Nestor’" (2013, ASAtene) analyzes the imagery of the Ring of Nestor in relation to Aegean forgeries and debates over authenticity. The abstract and AI-generated key takeaways indicate that the study revisits specific iconographic features and comparative material to reassess prior interpretations of the ring’s motifs and their significance in Minoan and Mycenaean art. Eliopoulos uses iconographic connections, such as incurved altars depicted on the ring, as arguments that support the ring’s authenticity despite earlier suspicions of forgery. The paper situates the Ring of Nestor and the Ring of Minos within a long history of scholarly controversy, noting that generations of scholars have questioned their genuineness, and it argues against dismissing unprovenanced rings outright, emphasizing their potential value for understanding ancient societies and material culture.

Andreas G. Vlachopoulos’s paper "The Ring of Nestor and the quest for authenticity" (Aegis 18, 2020) focuses on establishing the authenticity of the Ring of Nestor (CMS VI, no. 277) and interpreting its complex iconography in the context of Late Bronze Age Aegean glyptic art. The abstract states that long-term research has led to documentation in favor of the ring’s authenticity and to a reassessment of earlier scholarly tendencies to label certain Creto‑Mycenaean gold rings, including the Ring of Nestor and the Ring of Minos, as fakes due to their obscure or legendary discovery circumstances. This reassessment is reinforced by recent finds of iconographic subjects with comparable motifs (such as wall paintings, gold rings, figurines, and ivories) and detailed study of the rings’ techniques and craftsmanship dated to the 16th–15th centuries BC. A key focus of the paper is the main pictorial unit on the Ring of Nestor: the creature previously described by Arthur Evans as a "watch-dog" or "dragon" guarding the "tree of the world" whose branches carry the ring’s unusually populous scene. Vlachopoulos identifies this creature as a scorpion, characterizing it as a major apotropaic symbol in Bronze Age Aegean iconography; in this interpretation, the scorpion kills the so‑called "Minoan Dragon" and provides a coherent reading of the ring’s iconography. The AI key takeaways further note the ring’s physical dimensions and emphasize that its authenticity is now supported against earlier 1920s claims of forgery.

Evans used the Homeric name "Nestor" to evoke the legendary king of Pylos and the broader Mycenaean world, rather than to claim a direct historical link to a particular individual. Subsequent catalogues and bibliographic entries follow Evans in treating "The Ring of Nestor" as the title of his study and as the conventional name of the ring at its centre. [9][10]

title: Discovery, provenance and repository
content:
Evans framed the Ring of Nestor within a "sepulchral treasure" of gold signet rings and bead seals that he associated with Thisb�ea in Boeotia, as indicated by the title of his work and the description in digitized editions. The treasure as presented in his study does not derive from a single excavated tomb with secure stratigraphic documentation, but rather from a collection of objects grouped and interpreted by Evans in the early 20th century. Subsequent scholarship has therefore treated the ring as unprovenanced in strict archaeological terms, even when discussing its possible origin in relation to sites such as Kakovatos, Mycenae, Archanes or the area of Pylos. [10][20]

One modern overview of Mycenaean civilization notes that a famous ring acquired by Evans, identified as the Ring of Nestor, comes "apparently" from the tholos tomb in Kakovatos, and explicitly observes that its authenticity is disputed. Another study refers to the ring's "alleged" provenance in Mycenae and uses this supposed connection to argue that its imagery should not be read as referring to Neopalatial Cretan rituals. In a different context, a gold ring called the Ring of Nestor is said to have been found in tholos tomb A at Archanes, Crete, in the mid�d01960s and housed in a museum there. These statements illustrate the range of proposed or reported findspots in the secondary literature and underscore that no single archaeological context commands universal acceptance. [12]

In an introduction to a lecture on "Pylos and Minoan Crete", the Ring of Nestor is described as a gold ring dated to about 1500 BC and located in the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford. A separate discussion of Evans's notebooks specifies that he made a drawing of the Ring of Nestor in his Knossos notebook, now held in the Ashmolean Museum, with the entry identifiable by box and page references. These notices, together with Evans's longstanding association with the Ashmolean, indicate that the ring central to his 1925 study is preserved in that museum, even though the detailed acquisition history and archaeological context remain opaque. [10]

Popular and journalistic accounts of the Griffin Warrior tomb at Pylos have sometimes characterized the Ring of Nestor as the only previously known gold signet ring from the vicinity of the Palace of Nestor, with a newly discovered ring from Tholos IV near the palace described as "the only other" gold signet ring from the area. However, these narratives do not supply primary excavation records for the Ring of Nestor itself and are part of a broader attempt to contextualize the Griffin Warrior finds within the history of research at Pylos. Within specialist iconographic studies, by contrast, the ring is more cautiously treated as unprovenanced, and its connection to Pylos is not asserted as a secure archaeological fact. [2]

title: Iconography and interpretations
content:

content:
